content: Arthritis encompasses over 100 distinct rheumatic diseases and conditions that primarily affect the joints, the surrounding tissues, and other connective tissues in the body. The specific symptoms, their severity, and their location can vary significantly depending on the type of arthritis. Most commonly, arthritis is characterized by pain and stiffness in and around one or more joints. These symptoms may develop gradually over time or appear suddenly. Certain forms of arthritis can also involve the immune system and internal organs, leading to systemic effects. The most prevalent form of arthritis in the United States is osteoarthritis, followed by gout, fibromyalgia, and rheumatoid arthritis. Currently, approximately 46 million Americans have been diagnosed with arthritis by their healthcare providers, and this number is expected to rise. Symptoms of Arthritis The symptoms of arthritis vary depending on the specific type. Generally, individuals with arthritis experience pain and stiffness in and around one or more joints. The onset of symptoms may be gradual or sudden. Arthritis is often a chronic condition, meaning symptoms may persist over time or fluctuate, with periods of worsening and improvement. Causes of Arthritis Arthritis involves the breakdown of cartilage, which is a protective tissue that allows joints to move smoothly and absorbs shock during activities like walking. When cartilage deteriorates, the bones within the joint may rub against each other, leading to pain, swelling (inflammation), and stiffness. Joint inflammation can result from several causes, including: Autoimmune diseases, where the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy tissues. Joint injuries, such as broken bones. General wear and tear on the joints over time. Infections caused by bacteria or viruses. In some cases, joint inflammation resolves once the underlying cause is treated. However, if the inflammation persists, it can lead to chronic arthritis. Arthritis can affect both men and women, with osteoarthritis being the most common type. Other notable types of arthritis include ankylosing spondylitis, gout, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Risk Factors for Arthritis Certain factors increase the likelihood of developing arthritis. These risk factors can be categorized as modifiable or non-modifiable: Non-modifiable risk factors: Age: The risk of developing most types of arthritis increases with age. Gender: Women are more likely to develop arthritis, with 60% of arthritis cases occurring in women. However, gout is more common in men. Genetics: Specific genes are associated with a higher risk of certain types of arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and ankylosing spondylitis. Modifiable risk factors: Overweight and obesity: Excess weight contributes to the onset and progression of knee osteoarthritis. Joint injuries: Damage to a joint can increase the risk of developing osteoarthritis in that joint. Infections: Certain microbial agents can infect joints and lead to arthritis. Occupation: Jobs involving repetitive knee bending or squatting are associated with an increased risk of knee osteoarthritis. When to Seek Medical Care If you experience pain, stiffness, or swelling in or around one or more joints, it is important to consult a healthcare provider. A specific diagnosis of the type of arthritis is crucial for determining the most appropriate treatment. While there is no cure for most types of arthritis, early diagnosis and proper management are essential, particularly for inflammatory forms of arthritis. For example, early use of disease-modifying drugs can alter the course of rheumatoid arthritis. Timely diagnosis and treatment can significantly reduce pain and prevent joint damage. Diagnosis of Arthritis A healthcare provider will perform a physical examination and review your medical history. During the physical exam, they may observe: Fluid accumulation around a joint. Warm, red, or tender joints. Difficulty moving a joint, referred to as limited range of motion. Some types of arthritis may cause joint deformities, which can indicate severe, untreated rheumatoid arthritis. Blood tests and joint X-rays are often conducted to rule out infections and other causes of arthritis. Additionally, a sample of joint fluid may be extracted with a needle and sent to a laboratory for analysis. Treatment Options The primary goals of arthritis treatment are to control pain, minimize joint damage, and improve or maintain joint function and quality of life. According to the American College of Rheumatology, treatment may include: Medications Non-pharmacologic therapies: Physical or occupational therapy. Use of splints or joint assistive devices. Patient education and support. Weight loss to reduce joint stress. Surgery in severe cases. Prognosis While some arthritis-related disorders can be completely cured with appropriate treatment, most forms of arthritis are chronic conditions that require long-term management. Complications Potential complications of arthritis include: Chronic pain. Disability. Difficulty performing daily activities. Prevention of Arthritis Preventive measures depend on the specific type of arthritis. Maintaining a healthy body weight has been shown to reduce the risk of developing osteoarthritis and gout. Protecting joints from injuries or overuse can also lower the risk of osteoarthritis.
